nameStory: The red-legged grasshopper gets its name from the distinctive reddish or orange coloration on its hind legs, especially the upper portions called the femurs. This bright leg color makes it stand out from many of its brown and green relatives, giving field observers an easy way to remember and identify this common hopper.
description: The red-legged grasshopper is one of New England's most abundant and widespread grasshoppers, belonging to the short-horned grasshopper family. These medium-sized hoppers typically measure about an inch to an inch and a half long, with sturdy bodies that range from brown to olive green. They're excellent jumpers thanks to their powerful hind legs, and like all short-horned grasshoppers, their antennae are relatively short and thick compared to their cricket cousins. You'll often hear them before you see them, as they make chirping sounds by rubbing their legs against their wings.

idTips.label: Red-orange hind legs
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive reddish, orange, or coral coloration on the upper portions of the back legs (femurs) - this is your best identification clue and feels smooth to the touch if you gently handle one

idTips.label: Body color variation
idTips.description: The main body can be brown, olive green, or grayish, often with darker markings or stripes running lengthwise - the coloration may change slightly with temperature and surroundings

idTips.label: Short, thick antennae
idTips.description: The antennae are noticeably shorter than the body length and feel relatively thick and sturdy compared to the thread-like antennae of crickets and katydids

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Medium-sized grasshoppers about 1-1.5 inches long with a robust, chunky build that feels solid and substantial when gently held

idTips.label: Wing length
idTips.description: Wings typically extend to about the tip of the abdomen or slightly beyond, with clear areas and darker veining visible when spread

idTips.label: Jumping behavior
idTips.description: Powerful jumpers that can leap many times their body length when disturbed, often making a clicking or buzzing sound during flight

habitat: Red-legged grasshoppers thrive in open, sunny areas throughout New England including fields, meadows, roadsides, gardens, and grassy clearings. They prefer areas with mixed vegetation where they can find both grasses and broadleaf plants to feed on, from sea level up into mountain meadows. You'll often find them in disturbed areas like old fields, vacant lots, and the edges of agricultural lands where the soil has been turned or grazed.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but young nymphs (which look like tiny wingless adults) are more common. Look for small, active hoppers without fully developed wings in grassy areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and easiest to find. This is the best time to observe their red legs and hear their characteristic chirping sounds during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, continuing to feed and mate. They become less active as temperatures drop and may be found sheltering in tall grass or leaf litter during cooler days.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts. Eggs overwinter in the soil and are not visible to casual observers until they hatch the following spring.

funFact: Red-legged grasshoppers are living weather stations - scientists use them to study climate change because they're so sensitive to temperature that their activity levels, development rates, and even behavior patterns shift measurably with even small changes in local weather conditions.
confusionNotes: Red-legged grasshoppers are most easily confused with other brown grasshoppers in the same genus, but the red or orange coloring on the hind legs is usually distinctive. Memory trick: 'Red legs, red-legged' - if you see that coral or reddish color on the back legs, you've likely found your species. Some other grasshoppers may have yellowish legs, but the warm red-orange tone is characteristic.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'short-horned' grasshoppers, this refers to their antennae, not actual horns. The family name comes from comparing their antennae to those of 'long-horned' grasshoppers (katydids), which have thread-like antennae that can be longer than their entire body. This species is so common and well-studied that it's often used in scientific research as a 'model organism' - essentially a representative example for understanding grasshopper biology in general.
compareHints: Among its Melanoplus relatives, the red-legged grasshopper is distinguished primarily by those characteristic red-orange hind legs, while the two-striped grasshopper has prominent light stripes down its back, and the differential grasshopper is noticeably larger with chevron markings on its hind legs. The migratory grasshopper can also have reddish legs but typically shows more yellow coloration overall and different wing patterns. Most other spur-throat grasshoppers in the region lack the distinctive red leg coloration that makes this species relatively easy to identify.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Melanoplus relatives in New England, the two-striped grasshopper is the only one with those distinctive twin pale stripes running down its back.
Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Pine Tree Spur-throat stands out for its strong association with coniferous trees, while most others prefer grasses and herbs in open meadows.
Among its Melanoplus relatives, the differential grasshopper is distinguished by its larger, more robust build and those characteristic dark leg markings.

Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Huckleberry Spur-throat is most reliably separated by habitat - Red-legged Grasshoppers prefer more open grassy areas, Two-striped Grasshoppers like agricultural fields, and Pine tree Spur-throats stick to coniferous areas.
